title: Computational Arbitrage in AI Model Markets
one_liner: If model providers charge different prices for different success rates, a broker can buy model calls from them, combine them, and resell verified answers for less while still making money.
lead: This paper studies a simple market fact. A customer does not care which model solved a task; the customer cares whether the answer is correct and what it costs. If several model providers sell access at different prices and with different success rates, another company can sit in the middle, buy model calls from those providers, and choose where to spend each dollar. That middle company is an arbitrageur. It does not train its own model. It earns money by routing each task to the cheapest path that is still likely to produce a verifiable answer under the customer's budget. The paper shows that this is already possible in a real coding benchmark, and then traces what happens to prices, profits, and entry barriers when such brokers appear.

problem.h2: Selling model access creates room for middlemen
paras: Suppose two providers sell access to models for a task with a verifiable outcome, such as fixing a GitHub issue and checking whether the tests pass. One provider may be cheap but miss often. Another may be costly but succeed more often. A customer may be willing to pay up to a fixed amount for a correct answer, but the customer may not know which provider gives the best cost-to-success tradeoff on that particular task.

If a broker can estimate those tradeoffs more carefully than the customer, the broker can buy calls from the providers and resell only the successful outcome. The key fact is that the broker prices a completed solution, while the providers price raw model calls. Those are not the same product. Once the products differ, price gaps appear. The paper asks when those gaps are large enough to support profit, how stable they remain outside one benchmark, and how they change the broader market.

callout.html: Providers price model usage one call at a time, but customers buy completed answers. That mismatch creates room for arbitrage.

panels.title: 1. Several providers sell access
panels.caption: Each provider posts a price per call, but each call has a different chance of solving the task.

panels.title: 2. A customer names a budget
panels.caption: The customer only wants a correct, checkable answer and will pay up to a limit.

panels.title: 3. The broker routes the task
panels.caption: The broker chooses where to spend the budget based on expected payoff, not brand loyalty.

panels.title: 4. Verified success is resold
panels.caption: The broker pays providers for attempts and charges the customer only for a verified result.

panels.title: 5. Prices move across the market
panels.caption: Once brokers compete, customers pay less and providers lose some pricing power.

steps.text: Estimate how often each model solves a verifiable task and how much each attempt costs.
Assume the customer pays for a correct answer up to a fixed budget, not for every failed try.
Choose which provider gets the first attempt, which one acts as fallback, and when to stop spending.
Compare the customer's payment with the broker's total spending on provider calls.
Analyze what happens when many brokers compete, because competition pushes them to give back more of the margin, and when model distillation creates cheaper copies that lower input costs.

paras: The paper changes the unit of sale. Instead of treating a model call as the product, it treats a verified solution as the product and uses provider calls only as ingredients.
object.object: the pricing layer between customers and model providers

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: expected profit per task
hidden.name: Expected margin after paying for all model calls
paras: The broker has to reason about a hidden average, not a single outcome. A cheap provider may fail on many tasks, and a costly provider may succeed often enough to justify its price. The broker therefore tracks expected profit per task, which means average customer payment minus average spending on all attempted calls. This number decides whether arbitrage exists at all.

That quantity matters because the broker does not need every task to be profitable. The broker needs the portfolio of tasks to be profitable on average. A routing plan that loses money on hard tasks can still work if easy tasks earn enough to cover them. The paper measures this in a verifiable domain, so success and failure are not vague judgments; the task either passes the check or it does not.

heat.caption: The dark cells are the terms that decide whether the broker earns money or burns budget.

reads.html: The hidden number is simple: after many tasks, did the broker collect more from customers than it spent on model calls?
The paper studies arbitrage margin under provider-specific costs, success probabilities, and routing rules, then asks how that margin changes under competition and distillation.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: resell success, not attempts
paras: Arbitrage works here because model providers and customers value different things. Providers charge for access to computation. Customers pay for a completed answer. If the broker can predict which provider sequence gives the cheapest path to a correct answer, the broker can transform raw calls into a higher-level service and keep the gap as profit.

The routing step matters because price alone is not enough. A model that costs half as much but succeeds one tenth as often is not actually cheaper per solved task, because many more failed attempts have to be paid for before one success arrives. The broker therefore combines price and success chance into one decision rule. In the case study, even simple rules earn money because they avoid paying premium prices on tasks that the cheaper model already handles well, while still keeping a fallback path for harder cases.

The market analysis matters because arbitrage changes incentives. If many brokers can undercut providers, customer prices fall because brokers compete away part of the gap. At the same time, smaller providers gain a path into the market because a broker can include them in a bundle before they are strong enough to win customers directly.

stages.s: Estimate each provider's cost and success rate
Choose first try and fallback order
Run calls until success or budget stop
Broker margin and new market prices

math.h2: The equation: revenue minus routed call cost
math.words: A broker earns money on a task when the payment for a verified answer is larger than the average amount spent across all provider calls used to get that answer.
symbols: average profit per task for the broker
what the customer pays for a successful verified answer
price of one call to a chosen provider
how often that provider is actually invoked under the routing rule

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Customer pays 10 dollars for a verified fix.
Cheap provider costs 2 dollars and solves 60 of 100 tasks.
Premium fallback costs 5 dollars and is used only on the 40 remaining tasks.
Expected margin is 10 - 4 = 6 dollars per task before other overhead.

math.note: The point is not a single task. The point is the average over many tasks under one routing policy.

charts.title: Direct purchase from one provider
charts.note: Without brokers, customers must choose one provider and absorb its full pricing policy.

charts.title: Brokered purchase with arbitrage
charts.note: The paper's case study reports margins up to about 40 percent, while the market analysis predicts lower customer prices and easier entry for smaller providers.

items.html: If the broker learned provider quality on one task mix and the market shifts, the routing rule can spend money in the wrong places because past win rates no longer describe current tasks.
The setup works best when success is easy to check. If the customer cannot verify quality cleanly, the broker can resell weak answers and the pricing logic becomes harder to trust.
Providers may change prices, bundle products, or limit access when brokers start extracting margin, because the source of profit is the gap between provider pricing and solution pricing.
Use a verifiable task, estimate success rates carefully, set a firm stop rule, and update the routing policy as prices and models change.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simulator with two providers, a task set with known success rates, and a customer who pays only for verified solutions. Let a broker choose between cheap-first, premium-first, and fallback routing rules. Track customer price, broker spending, and broker profit across many tasks. Then add a second broker and show that customer prices move downward because the brokers compete away part of the margin.
demo.closing: The demo should make one point visible: the broker wins when it prices solved tasks while buying raw model calls below that solved-task value.
